title: Seagrass meadows: what they are, what they do, how much carbon they store, and why they are being lost

sources.title: Five ways often-unheralded seagrasses boost biodiversity

sources.publisher: NOAA Office of National Marine Sanctuaries
sources.title: Seagrass Meadows

facts.text: Seagrasses are flowering plants that grow underwater in shallow coastal areas where sunlight reaches the seafloor.
Unlike seaweeds, which are algae, seagrasses have true roots, leaves, flowers, and seeds.
Dense seagrass leaves slow water movement, trap sediment, and help keep coastal water clear.
Seagrass reduces wave energy, which helps protect coasts from floods and storms.
Seagrass meadows are nursery habitats for young fish; they support about 20 per cent of the world's largest fisheries.
Seagrass meadows give shelter and food to many species, including sea turtles and dugongs.
Seagrass meadows cover only about 0.1 per cent of the ocean floor but store up to 18 per cent of the world's oceanic carbon.
An estimated 7 per cent of seagrass meadows are lost worldwide each year.
Major causes of seagrass loss include coastal development, poor water quality from runoff, and rising ocean temperatures.
Boat propellers and anchors can tear up and scar seagrass meadows.
Boat-mooring programs, which let boats tie up instead of dropping anchor, along with cleaner water, give damaged meadows a chance to recover.
